explain: The pattern matched; the entropy filter rejected the value because human-chosen passwords are not random. That filter is what keeps scanners usable on large codebases, at the price of missing exactly the weakest passwords.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Dynamic secrets and leases: credentials that expire on their own
question: An attacker copies a dynamic credential from an app's debug log. The app keeps renewing the lease every 50 minutes (TTL 1 h, max TTL 24 h). How long can the attacker use the copy?
options: At most 1 hour
Forever, because renewal resets the maximum
Not at all, because dynamic credentials are bound to the app's IP address
Until the lease reaches its 24-hour maximum or someone revokes it, because the app's renewals keep the same credential alive
explain: Renewal extends the same username and password, so the attacker benefits from it. The max TTL is the hard stop. Dynamic database credentials are not bound to a network address unless the database itself enforces that, so revoke the lease as soon as misuse is seen.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Key ceremonies: the DNS root key and multi-person control
question: Which control in the root KSK design stops the same small group from both activating the HSM and restoring its keys elsewhere?
options: Separate roles with separate quorums: Crypto Officers activate, Recovery Key Share Holders restore
Tamper-evident bags
Quarterly ceremonies
FIPS level 3 HSMs
explain: Separation of duties: the people who can switch the key on are not the people who can rebuild it, so an attacker must corrupt both groups. The other controls protect the hardware and the schedule.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Taint by hand: following one value from source to sink
question: Which of these is a correct sanitizer for a value that will become part of a SQL query string?
options: `html.escape(value)`
`value.strip()`
`int(value)`, used only where a number is expected
`value.replace("'", "")`
explain: int() can only return a number, which cannot contain SQL syntax, so its output is safe for that sink. html.escape targets HTML, strip() removes only whitespace, and deleting quotes is a blocklist that breaks names like O'Brien and misses injection that needs no quote. Parameterised queries remain the better fix.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Regular expressions that hang: ReDoS and the Cloudflare outage
question: Which pattern is the ReDoS risk when matched against long user input in JavaScript?
options: `^https://example\.com/`
explain: `(\d+)+` nests one quantifier inside another, so a long run of digits followed by a non-digit has exponentially many ways to fail. The others have bounded or unambiguous structure: each character can be matched in only one way.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Apple goto fail: one duplicated line in C
question: Which single defence would most reliably have caught goto fail before release, according to the sources in this lesson?
options: A longer code freeze before each iOS release
Renaming the label from fail to cleanup
A negative test that connects to a server whose handshake is signed with the wrong key
Running the code under AddressSanitizer
explain: A test that must fail (bad signature) would have passed instead, exposing the bug immediately; Langley built exactly such a test server. AddressSanitizer finds memory errors, and this was a logic error with no bad memory access. Renaming and code freezes change nothing.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Rust: what safe Rust promises, and reviewing unsafe
question: The CVE-2021-31162 proof of concept contained `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. What does that show?
options: The attribute does not work
Rust has no memory safety guarantees
Undefined behaviour can come from unsafe code in libraries you call, including std, not just your own
Panics are always memory errors
explain: forbid(unsafe_code) guaranteed the program itself had no unsafe blocks; the double free was inside the standard library's own unsafe implementation of Vec::from_iter. The guarantee covers your code, and relies on the soundness of everything beneath it.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Writing the finding and the fix so it gets merged
question: You found SQL injection in an internal admin-only report page that runs with a read-only database account. How should severity be described?
options: Critical: SQL injection is always critical
Informational: admins can be trusted
Reachable only by admins and limited to reads by the account's permissions: lower than the same bug on a public page, but still a real finding to fix
Not a finding, because the account is read-only
explain: Severity combines impact and reachability. Admin-only access and a read-only account both reduce it, but a compromised admin session or a malicious insider could still read data they should not. Say exactly that, and recommend parameterisation anyway.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IKEv2: four messages to build the keys and the first tunnel
question: At which point can both IKEv2 peers compute the encryption keys for the IKE SA?
options: After message 2, once both Diffie-Hellman values and nonces have been exchanged
After message 4, once both AUTH payloads have been verified
Before message 1, from the pre-shared key alone
Only after the first ESP packet arrives
explain: SKEYSEED depends on the Diffie-Hellman secret and both nonces, all known after IKE_SA_INIT. That is why messages 3 and 4 can already be encrypted. Authentication comes later, in IKE_AUTH.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: SSH's transport layer: version, KEXINIT, key exchange and host keys
question: In OpenSSH 10.3's debug output, what does "kex: algorithm: mlkem768x25519-sha256" tell an auditor?
options: The session uses a hybrid of ML-KEM-768 and X25519 for key agreement, so recorded traffic resists a future quantum computer
The host key is a post-quantum signature key
The connection uses no Diffie-Hellman at all
The MAC algorithm is SHA-256 based on ML-KEM
explain: The kex line names the key agreement method only. Host keys are reported separately (here ssh-ed25519, still classical). The hybrid includes X25519 Diffie-Hellman alongside ML-KEM.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: SNMPv3: managing devices without a password in every packet
question: An auditor finds SNMPv3 configured at the authNoPriv level. What does that protect, and what does it not?
options: It encrypts the data but does not authenticate the sender
It authenticates messages and blocks replays, but the values (configurations, counters) travel unencrypted
It provides no protection; it is the same as SNMPv2c
It protects everything, because authentication implies encryption
explain: authNoPriv adds an HMAC and the timeliness check, so forged and replayed messages are rejected, but there is no privacy: anyone on the path can read the payload. authPriv adds encryption.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Choosing and auditing secure protocols, and the post-quantum plan
question: A company runs a strong IKEv2 configuration with certificates, but its VPN gateway's web login page has an unpatched authentication bypass. Which statement is right?
options: The gateway is at risk: an internet-facing appliance can be compromised through its software, whatever protocol it speaks
The VPN is safe because the IPsec cryptography is strong
Only users who log in through the web page are at risk
IKEv2 encrypts the web login page, so the bug cannot be reached
explain: The protocol and the product are separate. Attackers have repeatedly taken over VPN appliances through bugs in their web components, then harvested credentials and moved inward. Patch and monitor the appliance itself.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Clark-Wilson: well-formed transactions and separation of duty
question: A developer runs a one-off UPDATE in the production accounts table to fix a customer's balance, without going through the application. Which Clark-Wilson rule does this break most directly?
options: C1: IVPs must validate CDIs
E3: users must be authenticated
C5: UDIs must be validated
E1: only certified TPs may change CDIs
explain: The developer changed a CDI without any certified TP. They were probably authenticated (E3 holds), the IVP may even pass by luck (C1), and no UDI was turned into a CDI by a TP (C5 is about TPs).

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Inside BeyondCorp: inventory, trust tiers and the access proxy
question: Google's migration put a user on enforcement only after over 99.99% of their traffic had been eligible for 30 days in logging mode. What problem does that rule solve?
options: It avoids breaking real work by enforcing before all of a user's workflows function through the new path
It prevents attackers from guessing the rules
It reduces bandwidth costs
It satisfies a legal requirement for 30 days of logs
explain: Logging mode shows exactly which traffic would be dropped. Waiting for near-complete eligibility means enforcement breaks almost nothing, and the leftover flows point to workflows that still need fixing or an exemption.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Case: VPN appliances under attack, Pulse 2021 and Ivanti 2024
question: Which design most limits the damage if the remote-access component at the edge is fully compromised?
options: A bigger VPN appliance with more CPU
A VPN that gives remote users the whole internal network, plus a strong perimeter firewall
Per-application access where each application verifies a signed, audience-bound identity assertion and users authenticate with phishing-resistant MFA at a separate identity provider
Hiding the VPN's address from public DNS
explain: Per-application access limits reach; app-side verification means a foothold at the edge is not trusted by default; phishing-resistant MFA at a separate identity provider means a hijacked edge page does not yield reusable passwords. Hiding the address is security by obscurity, and internet-wide scans find it anyway.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Running a security design review
question: Which finding is written so that an engineer can act on it?
options: "The design violates zero trust."
"Least privilege is not followed."
"The reporting role has UPDATE on invoices (grant in db/roles.sql line 14); move reporting to a read-only replica; owner data-team; before Q1."
"Consider improving database security."
explain: It states the risk in system terms, gives checkable evidence, recommends a specific change, and assigns an owner and a deadline. The others name principles or vague goals without saying what to change.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Idempotent steps: designing work that is safe to run twice
question: Which step is NOT idempotent as written?
options: Set case tag 'vpn-spray'
Disable account j.doe
Look up 203.0.113.7 in the intel cache
Append 'enrichment done' to the case notes
explain: Each append adds another note, so running it twice leaves two notes. Setting a tag and disabling an account reach the same state however often they run, and a lookup changes nothing.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: LLM-assisted triage: the model advises, code and people decide
question: The model replies {suggestion: likely_benign, evidence: [{field: src.owner, value: corporate scanner}]}, but the alert has no src.owner field. What should the pipeline do?
options: Accept it: the model may know the scanner from its training data
Add a src.owner field to the alert so the evidence matches
Close the alert, since evidence was provided
Reject the reply, log it as a confabulation, and leave the alert with the analyst without AI advice
explain: Evidence that is not in the alert is invented, whatever the model's confidence. Editing the alert to fit the model corrupts the record, and closing on a rejected reply is the outcome the check exists to prevent.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: When not to automate, and a design review checklist
question: Which step fits 'robot prepares, human approves'?
options: Adding asset and identity context to every new alert
Opening a case for each new alert
Sending the company-wide breach notification email
Isolating one employee laptop from the network after a confirmed malicious download
explain: Isolation disrupts one person and is awkward to undo, so a quick human check is worth it, but the blast radius is one machine and speed matters. Enrichment and case creation are safe to automate fully; a company-wide breach notice is a human decision from start to finish.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who attacks and why: criminals, states, insiders, activists
question: A company's main worry is ransomware affiliates. Which control best reduces that specific threat?
options: A bigger firewall rule set for outbound web traffic only
Hiding the company's logo from its website
Encrypting the data at rest on servers
Offline backups plus removing unused remote-access accounts
explain: Affiliates commonly enter through exposed remote access with stolen credentials and profit by making data unavailable. Removing unused access shrinks their entry points, and offline backups (which CISA's DarkSide advisory recommends) remove the leverage. Encryption at rest does not stop ransomware from encrypting the data again.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Equifax 2017: a known bug and a missed patch
question: Struts 2.5.10 is installed. Is it vulnerable to CVE-2017-5638?
options: No: 2.5.10 is newer than 2.3.32
No: only 2.3.x was affected
It depends on the CVSS score
Yes: on the 2.5 branch the first fixed version is 2.5.10.1
explain: NVD lists 2.5.x before 2.5.10.1 as affected. Comparing across branches (2.5.10 against 2.3.32) is the classic mistake; compare within the branch.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The legal and ethical line: authorisation and disclosure
question: Under the Supreme Court's reading in Van Buren, which act most clearly 'exceeds authorized access'?
options: An employee reads a report they are allowed to read, for a personal reason
A user forgets to log out
A researcher reads a public security.txt file
A logged-in user changes an ID in a URL to open another customer's records that are off-limits to them
explain: The Court tied 'exceeds authorized access' to entering areas of a computer, such as files or databases, that are off-limits to you. Reading another customer's records fits; misusing data you may see is the case the Court excluded.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: From gaps to a roadmap: strategy, sequencing and dependencies
question: Which statement is a strategy rather than a wish?
options: We will be world-class in security
We will improve our posture across all areas this year
For 12 months identity and recovery come first; we will not start a DLP programme this year
Security is everyone's responsibility
explain: Only that option contains a diagnosis-driven choice and an explicit thing not to do, which lets people decide what to stop asking for. The others cannot guide a single resource decision.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Designing the team: functions, coverage and where people sit
question: Why does one 24x7 seat need about 5 people rather than 168 / 40 = 4.2?
options: Because night shifts are shorter by law
Because MDR vendors require it
Because each analyst actually works fewer than 52 x 40 hours once leave, holidays, sickness and training are removed
Because the script rounds up twice
explain: 168 / 40 assumes every person works every week of the year. With 48 days away (in the example), one person works 1,696 hours, so 8,760 / 1,696 = 5.17, rounded up to 6 people.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Regulators and disclosure: materiality, risk factors, certifications
question: Under NYDFS Part 500 as amended in 2023, who signs the annual certification of compliance?
options: Any senior officer
The external auditor
The board chair alone
The highest-ranking executive and the CISO
explain: Section 500.17(b)(2) requires the highest-ranking executive and the CISO (or, without a CISO, the senior officer responsible for the programme). It must rest on documentation kept for five years.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Writing a finding: title, impact, evidence, fix
question: Which finding title is most useful in a ticket list read by an engineering manager?
options: Critical vulnerability found during testing
Burp Suite scanner result #44
CVE-style issue in API
Missing ownership check on /api/invoices/{id} exposes all customers' invoices
explain: It names the weakness, the location and the consequence, so the manager can route it and judge urgency without opening it. The others say nothing about what or where.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Risk memos and exceptions: making someone own the decision
question: Who should sign a risk acceptance for an unpatched customer-facing system?
options: The security engineer who found it
Whoever is on call that week
Nobody; acceptances should be verbal
The designated risk owner, who is accountable for the business outcome and has authority to accept it
explain: NIST IR 8286 defines the risk owner as the party responsible and accountable. Security advises and records; the owner decides. A security engineer accepting business risk is deciding something they do not own.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Getting a fix shipped when you cannot order it
question: A team ignores a High finding for six weeks. What is the most effective next message?
options: A broadcast email to the whole engineering department
Silently lower the severity so the backlog looks better
Fix it yourself in production without telling them
A message to the team lead offering the ready fix or an exception, with a date, and naming the pre-agreed escalation if neither happens
explain: It makes the cheapest path obvious, gives the owner a real choice including a formal exception, and uses a known escalation route rather than public shaming or unilateral action.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Inside the search tree: selection, expansion, evaluation and backup
question: In a two-player search, the backup adds +v to every edge on the path, where v is the value for the player to move at the leaf. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; Q is symmetric between players
The search spends too many visits on the prior
Every second level is credited from the wrong player's view, so selection there favors moves that help the opponent
Visit counts stop growing
explain: The player to move at the leaf did not choose the last edge; the opponent did. Crediting that edge with +v rewards the opponent's move for being good for you. Flipping the sign at each ply keeps every Q in the chooser's point of view.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Playing against your past self: SPIN and Self-Rewarding LMs
question: In SPIN's idealized update, set lambda = 1. What happens after one iteration?
options: The model moves halfway toward the data distribution
The model becomes exactly p_data, and further iterations change nothing
The model overshoots p_data and oscillates
Nothing, because lambda = 1 cancels the loss
explain: With 1/lambda = 1 the update is p_t times p_data / p_t, which is p_data after renormalizing. Then the ratio is 1 everywhere and the update is the identity. Real training cannot represent the ideal update exactly, which is one reason SPIN needs several iterations.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Adversarial self-play for language models, and AlphaProof
question: AlphaProof's training problems come from an auto-formalizer that sometimes mistranslates the original problem. Why does this not corrupt the training signal?
options: Mistranslated statements are removed by a human reviewer
Any Lean statement is a real problem: Lean checks whatever proof or disproof is found, so each attempt is labeled correctly even if it is not the intended problem
The value head learns to ignore mistranslated problems
Test-time RL replaces the main RL data
explain: The paper notes that each auto-formalized statement, faithful or not, is a valid formal problem to prove or disprove. The judge, Lean's kernel, is exact about the statement actually given, so the experience is always correctly labeled.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Provider prompt caching is a different thing from semantic caching
question: Your self-hosted RAG service retrieves the same popular chunks for many questions, but in a different order each time. The server's prefix cache hits only on the system prompt. What can reuse the chunks' computed state?
options: A longer prefix-cache lifetime
A semantic cache keyed on the user's question
A higher similarity threshold
Non-prefix KV reuse in the style of CacheBlend, which recomputes a few tokens of each reused chunk
explain: A longer lifetime does not change the exact-prefix rule, and the semantic cache reuses whole answers, not chunk computation, so it does nothing for new questions. CacheBlend reuses each chunk's KV cache in any position and recomputes the small set of tokens whose KV deviates most, restoring the attention between chunks.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Question-aware and learned compression: LongLLMLingua and LLMLingua-2
question: Your requests have a stable 3,000-token system prompt (served from the provider's prompt cache) followed by 30,000 tokens of retrieved documents that change per question. Where should question-aware compression go?
options: On the whole prompt, system prompt included
On the system prompt only, because it is sent on every request
Only on the model's output
On the retrieved documents only, leaving the cached system prompt untouched
explain: The retrieved text is long, mostly irrelevant to any one question, and differs per request anyway, which is what LongLLMLingua targets. Compressing the system prompt per question would change the prefix and lose the 0.1x cache reads while saving little.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: IMDSv2: session tokens, PUT and a hop limit of 1
question: An attacker has remote code execution on an EC2 instance that requires IMDSv2 with a hop limit of 1. Can they read the role credentials?
options: No: the token requirement blocks them
No: the TTL of 1 drops the token
Only if the instance has a public IP address
Yes: code on the instance can send its own PUT, receive the token directly and use it
explain: IMDSv2 protects against requests relayed by something else (WAFs, proxies, SSRF, routers). Code running on the instance is exactly the legitimate client IMDS is built to serve. That is why role permissions must still follow least privilege.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Insecure deserialization: when loading data runs code
question: A Java service checks `if (!(obj instanceof Cart)) throw ...` right after `readObject()`. Why does this not stop a gadget chain?
options: instanceof is slow
The chain runs inside readObject, while the object graph is being built, before the check executes
Gadget chains only affect PHP
Cart must implement Externalizable
explain: Deserialization hooks run as each object is reconstructed. By the time readObject returns and your check runs, any side effect has already happened. Filters must act before construction, which is what ObjectInputFilter does.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Path traversal and safe path joins
question: What is the strongest design for a "download your invoice" endpoint?
options: Accept a file name and strip every dot and slash
Accept an invoice ID, check the user owns it, look up the stored path server-side, and never put user text in a path
Accept a full path but only allow paths ending in .pdf
Accept a file name and URL-decode it twice before checking
explain: If user input never reaches the filesystem API, there is nothing to traverse, and the ownership check also closes the IDOR hole from the access-control course. Extension checks and character stripping are both known to be bypassable.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: LM programs: why the runtime should see the whole program
question: Why does the interpreter send the shared prefix to the runtime before the fork branches?
options: So that the prefix is computed and inserted into the radix tree once; branches arriving together would otherwise each find nothing cached and each prefill it
Because the runtime cannot accept prompts longer than the prefix
To let the runtime pick a different model for each branch
Because RadixAttention only works when requests arrive one at a time
explain: If both branches arrive at the same moment with nothing cached, each matches zero tokens and each computes the shared part. The paper calls the fix a frontend hint: it simplifies runtime matching and is one of the co-design benefits in its ablation.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Structured output today: grammar masks inside the SGLang scheduler
question: Your application needs an EBNF grammar for a small domain-specific language. Which `--grammar-backend` cannot serve it?
options: xgrammar
outlines
llguidance
None of them: SGLang supports only JSON schema
explain: The docs list EBNF support for XGrammar and llguidance; Outlines in SGLang supports JSON schema and regex only.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Dijkstra's algorithm: settle nodes in order of distance
question: A teammate stops Dijkstra as soon as T is first inserted into the queue, to save time. Using the toy run, why is this a bug in general?
options: It is not a bug; the first label any node receives is final
It only matters when the graph has negative weights
Insertion happens after settling, so the check never fires
Tentative labels can still drop after insertion, as C did (7 from S, then 6 via D)
explain: A label is only final when its node is popped as the queue minimum. C first got 7 directly from S and later improved to 6 through D. The same can happen to t, so the stop test must be on the pop, not the push.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
question: Why does an edge-based (arc-based) graph make turn costs routable with an unchanged Dijkstra?
options: It deletes all intersections, so turns no longer exist
It stores turn costs in the heuristic
It merges parallel roads into one vertex
Its vertices are road segments, so a turn is an ordinary weighted arc between two segments
explain: Once a state is the road you are on, the cost of turning from it onto the next road is just an arc weight, and plain Dijkstra applies. The price is a larger graph: 28 directed segments instead of 9 junctions in the toy.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: IIR filters, zero-phase filtering and real sensor data
question: A 20 s recording at 50 Hz shows a spectral peak at 1.5 Hz. The bins are 0.05 Hz apart. A colleague wants 0.01 Hz precision on the rate. What is the honest way to get finer frequency resolution?
options: Record a longer segment (100 s gives 0.01 Hz bins)
Raise the sampling rate to 250 Hz
Zero-pad to 5000 samples, which gives true 0.01 Hz resolution
Use a causal Butterworth filter before the FFT
explain: Resolution is 1/duration, so 0.01 Hz needs about 100 s of data. A higher fs only extends the frequency range. Zero-padding interpolates between bins (useful to locate a single clean peak more precisely) but does not separate close frequencies, as Smith points out.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Masks instead of branches: compares, blends and AVX-512
question: Your AVX2 select gives out[i] = 2x for x = NaN lanes on one machine and 0 on another build. Which part of the code is the likely suspect?
options: The blendv argument order
The compare predicate (ordered versus unordered)
movemask
loadu versus load
explain: An ordered predicate like _CMP_GT_OQ returns false when an input is NaN, so NaN lanes become 0; an unordered predicate such as _CMP_NLE_UQ (not less-or-equal) returns true for NaN. If two builds use different predicates or a compiler rewrites the comparison under -ffast-math, NaN handling changes.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
question: A server bump-allocates parsed headers into a per-request arena and resets it when the response is sent. A cache stores a pointer to one parsed header so later requests can reuse it. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, because resetting the arena only moves a pointer and does not change the bytes
Memory leaks, because the header is never freed
The cached pointer dangles: after reset the next request bump-allocates over the same bytes
The arena must be locked, because a bump pointer cannot be reset while other pointers exist
explain: Reset makes the whole chunk free again, and the very next request reuses those addresses. The cached pointer now aliases unrelated data. Objects that outlive the phase must be copied out (or allocated elsewhere).

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Three modules, one loop: how slime is laid out
question: A colleague changes `--hf-checkpoint` to point at the latest exported checkpoint every time they resume training, "so SGLang starts from the right weights". Is this needed?
options: Yes, otherwise SGLang samples from the original weights for the whole run
Only for MoE models
No: train.py syncs the Megatron weights into SGLang before the first rollout
No, because SGLang reads Megatron's torch_dist checkpoint directly
explain: The usage guide says slime synchronizes parameters from Megatron to SGLang before the first training step, so the HF checkpoint initializes SGLang (architecture, tokenizer, initial tensors) rather than carrying trained weights. Its config still matters for quantized rollout (lesson 4). SGLang does not read torch_dist checkpoints.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: The trainer side: from scored samples to a policy-gradient step
question: A run uses `--advantage-estimator grpo --kl-coef 0.05`, hoping to keep the policy near the reference. The reference model loads and slime computes a per-token KL, yet training behaves exactly like a run without KL. Why?
options: The KL is computed against the wrong checkpoint
--kl-coef is ignored unless --colocate is set
The coefficient is too small to matter
--kl-coef only shapes rewards for ppo and REINFORCE++; GRPO's advantages ignore it. Use --use-kl-loss --kl-loss-coef instead
explain: compute_advantages_and_returns computes the KL whenever kl_coef is non-zero, but get_grpo_returns copies only the reward to every token. GRPO's KL term goes into the loss, and slime asserts that kl_coef and kl_loss_coef are not both set.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: What a blockchain is: a shared ledger that nobody owns
question: In the toy chain, an attacker edits block 0 and also recomputes block 0's digest. What does the checker report?
options: Every block is ok, because block 0's digest is correct again
Block 1 is broken, because it still stores the old digest of block 0
Only block 2 is broken
Nothing can be checked once a digest changes
explain: Block 1 stores the previous digest e7a83d, but block 0 now hashes to b3efbf. The attacker would have to rewrite block 1, then block 2, and so on to the tip.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: A toy chain in Python, and thinking in invariants
question: In the toy chain, a function moves 3 ETH to Bo and then raises Revert. What does Bo end up with?
options: The 3 ETH, because the transfer completed before the error
Half, as a partial refund
It depends on whether Bo is a contract
Nothing extra: the revert restores the balances saved when the call began
explain: Calls are atomic: the snapshot taken at the start of the call is restored. The EVM behaves the same way, which is also what makes flash loans possible (lesson 10).

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Price oracles, spot prices and flash loans
question: A lending protocol values collateral with the spot price of a deep AMM pool. A reviewer says the pool is too deep to manipulate. What is wrong with that argument?
options: Deep pools cannot be manipulated at all, so nothing
AMMs have no spot price
Only TWAP oracles can be flash-loaned
Flash loans supply enormous capital for one transaction, so depth raises the cost but does not remove the attack
explain: Depth sets how much capital a price move needs; flash loans make that capital free for one transaction. The attack works whenever the profit exceeds fees and slippage.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Bridges: where many of the largest DeFi thefts happened
question: Which change most directly prevents the Nomad failure?
options: Raising gas limits
Adding more validators
Rejecting the zero root explicitly, so a default value can never be a trusted one
Moving to proof of stake
explain: The bug was that an unset value equalled a trusted value. Explicitly refusing the zero root (and testing upgrades against 'unproven message' cases) closes it whatever the validator setup.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Incident response on chain, and where to practise
question: Why does monitoring the bridge's invariant matter even after the bug is already being exploited?
options: It reverses the stolen transactions
It identifies the attacker's real name
It is required for an audit
Many exploits repeat over many transactions or blocks (Nomad's copycats); detecting the first one and pausing stops the rest
explain: On-chain theft is often spread over many transactions. Fast detection plus a pause turns a total loss into a partial one, as the toy run shows (60 versus 10).

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Enrichment: asset, identity and intel context, and where it lies
question: Enrichment says the source IP of a failed-login burst is "malicious (feed-A, last seen 2 years ago)" and geolocates to a mobile carrier. What is the soundest reading?
options: Confirmed attacker; block the IP everywhere
Weak evidence: the intel is old and carrier IPs are shared by many subscribers, so judge the alert on the login pattern itself
Definitely benign, because carrier IPs are always legitimate users
Ignore the alert, since enrichment disagrees with itself
explain: Both enrichment facts are weak: stale reputation, and an address that many unrelated customers share. Blocking it could cut off your own mobile users (collateral damage, in RFC 6269's words). The behaviour in the logs is better evidence than the label.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Cloud key misuse, and what Snowflake customers could see in 2024
question: GuardDuty raises InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS for a web server's role credentials. The source IP is the company's own on-premises VPN gateway, and the web team confirms the server routes outbound traffic through it. What is the right outcome?
options: Benign true positive: document it and add a suppression rule scoped to that finding type and the gateway's IP range
True positive: rotate everything and escalate
False positive: disable GuardDuty
Ignore it; GuardDuty will learn the behaviour anyway
explain: This is the benign case AWS describes, and AWS recommends exactly a two-criteria suppression rule. Letting the model learn it silently is worse: you lose the record of why, and anything later using that same remote address, including a real attacker behind the gateway, would stop producing findings.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Talking to users, owners and leaders during an investigation
question: You suspect an employee is copying customer data to a personal cloud account. Who do you contact first?
options: The employee, to hear their side
Their manager, by email
The incident lead and, through them, HR and legal, keeping the case need-to-know
The whole security team channel
explain: Possible insider cases are sensitive: contacting the employee or a wide channel can tip them off, harm an innocent person, or break legal process. The NCSC advises segregating insider threat work for exactly these reasons.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Why Johnny can't encrypt: usability is a security property
question: In the study, seven participants encrypted messages to their team with their own public key. What kind of failure was this?
options: A bug in PGP's encryption code
Participants were not motivated to finish the task
The team members' email software was misconfigured
A mismatch between the user's mental model of keys and how public-key encryption works, with no feedback showing the error
explain: PGP encrypted exactly as asked. The users misunderstood whose key to use, and the interface gave no warning until the team replied that they could not read the message.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a pretext: how manipulation is built and broken
question: An attacker offers employees free 'priority IT support' if they install a remote access tool. Which form in NIST's list is this?
options: Thread-jacking
Quid pro quo
Tailgating
Baiting
explain: Quid pro quo offers a service or favour in return for an action. Baiting leaves an object as a lure; thread-jacking hijacks an existing email conversation; tailgating is physical.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: SIM swaps, bribed insiders and people you do not employ
question: The CSRB found Lapsus$ paid insiders at telecom providers. Why is that hard to counter with technical controls alone?
options: The insider uses legitimate access, so the action looks like normal work
Insiders always use encrypted messages
Telecom systems have no logs
Bribes are legal in some countries
explain: An insider approving an MFA request or doing a SIM swap is using tools they are allowed to use. Least privilege, strong customer authentication before sensitive actions, and reporting channels matter more than filters.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Dropped USB drives, implants and unattended screens
question: A keyboard-class USB device appears on a finance PC at 02:00 while the screen is locked and no one badged into the floor. What should the SOC conclude first?
options: The user bought a new keyboard
Device control is working
Nothing, as the screen is locked
A possible physical intrusion with a hardware addition; isolate the host and check badge logs and CCTV
explain: The combination of time, locked screen and no badge entry points to someone physically present who should not be. A locked screen does not stop a device from being plugged in or a network implant from working.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Why single neurons are hard to read: superposition
question: In the pentagon model, which input is decoded wrongly with b = -0.309?
options: Only f1 on
f1 and f2 on (neighbours)
f1 and f3 on (non-neighbours)
No feature on
explain: Non-neighbours have cosine -0.809, so their sum cancels most of each one's own signal (0.191 each) while the shared neighbour f2 gets 0.618. After the bias only f2 survives. Neighbours reinforce each other instead.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Reading a latent: activating examples, logit effects, autointerp
question: An explanation scores 0.95 on simulation using only top-activating excerpts, but 0.30 when the excerpts are sampled across the whole activation range. What is the best reading?
options: The explanation fits the strongest activations but not the weaker ones that make up most firings; it is too narrow
The latent is dead
The simulator model is broken; trust the 0.95
The latent must be monosemantic because 0.95 is high
explain: Top examples can make a latent look cleaner than it is. Towards Monosemanticity and Paulo et al. sample across activation intervals precisely because weaker activations often follow a broader or different pattern.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: train a TopK SAE on GPT-2, then use a released one
question: Your SAE has FVU 0.19 and loss recovered 97.9% (zero ablation) at this residual site. Which extra number best tells you whether it is good enough to splice into the model for an analysis?
options: Its L0, because sparser is always better
The number of latents
Delta LM loss in nats (here about 0.2), compared with what your analysis can tolerate
The decoder norms
explain: Zero-ablating the residual stream is so destructive that loss recovered looks excellent for almost any SAE. Delta LM loss says directly how much worse the spliced model predicts text; 0.2 nats is a large degradation.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in map coordinates
question: A data scientist fits a GP to sensor data with an RBF kernel plus a white noise kernel. In kriging vocabulary, the white noise variance corresponds to:
options: The range
The sill
The nugget
The Lagrange multiplier
explain: A white noise term adds variance only on the diagonal, exactly like a nugget: semivariance jumps from 0 to the nugget as soon as two points are distinct.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
question: Which pair of models has the higher acceptance rate beta for a single position?
options: Both are equal because both drafts put most mass on the first token
explain: beta = sum of min(p, q). First pair: 0.5 + 0.1 = 0.6. Second pair: 0.5 + 0.4 = 0.9. What matters is overlap with the target, not agreeing on the top token.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: EAGLE drafts and prompt lookup decoding
question: Medusa's typical acceptance, Medusa-2, EAGLE-2 and prompt lookup: which of these can change the output distribution compared to the original target model?
options: Only EAGLE-2
Typical acceptance and Medusa-2
Prompt lookup, because copied tokens skip the target
All four
explain: Typical acceptance replaces rejection sampling with a threshold, and Medusa-2 fine-tunes the backbone itself. EAGLE-2 and prompt lookup only change how drafts are proposed; verification with the standard rule keeps the target's distribution.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
question: You pass 12 s of audio to Whisper. What does the encoder process?
options: A 80 x 1200 spectrogram, 600 positions
A 80 x 3000 spectrogram, 1500 positions, with the last 18 s padded with zeros
Three 4 s chunks processed in parallel
The raw 192,000 samples directly
explain: Whisper always feeds the encoder 30 s: the low-level API pads the audio to 480,000 samples, and `transcribe` pads each log-mel window to 3000 frames, so the shape is always 80 x 3000 and the stem always yields 1500 positions. The padded tail is silence, which matters later when we look at hallucinations.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The map of a process: segments, /proc/PID/maps and ASLR
question: A machine runs with `kernel.randomize_va_space = 1`. Across runs of a PIE program, which region keeps the same position relative to the program's own data segment?
options: The [heap], because heap randomization is only added at setting 2
The [stack]
Shared libraries such as libc
The [vdso]
explain: Setting 1 randomizes the mmap base, the stack and the vdso (so libraries move too) and the PIE code start; the data segment moves with the code. Only setting 2 adds heap randomization, so at 1 the heap starts right where bss ends, run after run.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
question: A 10 GiB Redis-like process (an in-memory key-value database) calls fork to write a snapshot while it keeps serving writes. Memory use climbs sharply during the snapshot. Why?
options: fork copies all 10 GiB up front
The child process leaks heap memory
Every page the parent writes while the child holds the old version triggers a copy-on-write fault and a new private copy
Copy-on-write is disabled for anonymous memory
explain: fork only duplicates page tables. But each page the parent modifies during the snapshot must be copied so the child still sees the old data, so memory grows with the number of distinct pages written. Huge pages make this worse: one small write can copy 2 MiB.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Difference of means: building a vector from contrast pairs
question: In the toy example, the single-pair direction from pair 4 still classifies all eight activations correctly. Why prefer the mean difference anyway?
options: It is the only direction with unit length
It makes projections of negatives exactly zero
Single-pair vectors cannot be added to the residual stream
It is closer to the true concept direction (cosine 0.991 vs 0.891), so steering along it changes less of everything else
explain: Classification only needs the right sign. Steering adds the whole vector, including its off-concept components. Pair 4's direction has a larger share of noise, so adding it would also push unrelated dimensions. The averaged vector is cleaner.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Lab: build, sweep and evaluate a steering vector on a small chat model
question: In the lab, c = +4 gave 0.805 and c = +8 gave 0.633 on test. Which conclusion is right?
options: The vector encodes the opposite behavior
Larger coefficients always help, so the test set must be mislabeled
Past some strength the added vector dominates the stream and disrupts the model, so the response curve turns over; choose c on validation and inspect side effects
Layer 14 was the wrong layer
explain: The steering direction is right (the curve is monotonic from -4 to +4), but at 8 times the vector (norm 8.6 against a stream of about 19) the push disrupts the model and answers drift back toward chance. ITI reports the same inverted U, and CAA saw large multipliers degrade open-ended text.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
question: Sensors publish at QoS 1. Your rollup job sums energy readings per minute and the totals are occasionally slightly too high. Most likely cause?
options: QoS 1 can lose messages, and losses push sums up
QoS 1 retries after a lost PUBACK, so a reading can be delivered twice and counted twice
Kafka reorders records within a partition
MQTT always runs over UDP, which duplicates packets
explain: At least once means no loss but possible duplicates. A sum counts a duplicate twice. The fix is to deduplicate on a reading id (device id plus sequence number) or to write results idempotently (so that writing the same result twice leaves the same outcome as writing it once), covered in the last lesson.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
question: Per Table 1 of the paper, for which sequences is one self-attention layer cheaper in total work than one recurrent layer?
options: Always, because it has O(1) sequential operations
When the sequence length n is larger than the model width d
When n is smaller than d, which is typical for sentence-length inputs
Never; it is only faster because of parallelism
explain: Self-attention costs about $n^2 d$ and a recurrent layer about $n d^2$, so attention does less total work when $n < d$. The paper notes this is most often the case for sentence representations in machine translation (the base model has d = 512). Sequential operations are a separate column: they measure parallelism, not total work.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding and the full encoder-decoder stack
question: Which sub-layer holds the most parameters in one base-model encoder layer?
options: Multi-head self-attention, because it has 8 heads
LayerNorm, because it has a gain and bias per dimension
The position-wise feed-forward network, about twice as many as attention
They are equal by design
explain: Attention: 4 x 512^2, about 1.05 million. FFN: 2 x 512 x 2048, about 2.10 million. LayerNorm has only 2 x 512 = 1,024 per instance. Heads split the attention width; they do not add parameters.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
question: Which statement about the paper's learning-rate schedule is correct?
options: It starts at its maximum and decays linearly to zero
It is constant at 1e-3 because Adam adapts the rate per parameter
It increases linearly for 4000 steps, then decays with the inverse square root of the step
It increases for the whole run
explain: Equation 3 is the minimum of a linear ramp and an inverse square root curve; the two meet at step = warmup = 4000, where the rate peaks at about 0.70e-3 for d_model = 512.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Relevance feedback: the full RSJ weight and query term counts
question: A pseudo-relevance feedback system expands every query from its top 10 results. For which query is it most likely to hurt?
options: An ambiguous query whose top 10 are mostly about the wrong meaning, so the added terms pull the search further off topic
A query whose top 10 are all relevant
A query with one very rare term
Any query, because blind feedback hurts on average
explain: Blind feedback assumes the top results are relevant. When they are, it finds useful new terms; when they are off topic, it adds that topic's words and drifts further away. The survey reports that it helps on average but fails on some queries, especially those whose first results are poor.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Which BM25? Variants, library differences and what they change
question: A paper reports BM25 nDCG@10 = 0.665 on SciFact; your BM25 gets 0.677. What is the most likely reason?
options: Your implementation has a bug, since BM25 is deterministic
SciFact's judgments changed between runs
Different k1, b, analyzer or field setup, which shift BM25 results more than the choice of variant
Your run used a dense retriever by mistake
explain: BM25 is deterministic for a fixed configuration, but configurations differ. BEIR used Anserini with k1 = 0.9, b = 0.4 and separate title and text fields; our pipeline gave 0.671 at those parameters and 0.677 at the Lucene defaults. Variant changes moved SciFact by under 0.005.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Assemble model.py and check it against GPT-2's real weights
question: After loading GPT-2's weights, your logits differ from Hugging Face's by at most 0.08 and every argmax agrees. Which cause fits best?
options: A missing transpose on attn.c_proj
The MLP uses exact GELU while GPT-2 was trained with the tanh approximation
Weight tying is missing
The causal mask is upper-triangular
explain: The two GELU formulas differ by a few ten-thousandths per activation, which adds up to small logit differences that rarely change the argmax; that is what we measured (0.080). A missing transpose gave a difference of 161.7 and degenerate text, and a flipped mask would leak the future and change the logits wildly.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Making it fast: TF32, bfloat16, torch.compile, fused attention and DDP
question: A run of GPT-2 124M processes 400,000 tokens per second on one GPU with a 989 TFLOP/s bf16 peak. Using 855 million FLOPs per token, what is its MFU?
options: About 86%
About 4%
About 35%
About 12%
explain: 400,000 x 855e6 = 3.42e14 FLOP/s, and 3.42e14 / 9.89e14 = 0.35. MFU compares useful model FLOPs to the hardware peak, the same calculation as for the A100 run.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
question: A model has 7 billion parameters and a scalar loss. How many numbers are in the gradient of the loss?
options: 1, because the loss is a single number
7 billion, one partial derivative per parameter
About 49 billion billion (7 billion squared), one per pair of parameters
It depends on the batch size
explain: The gradient has one entry per input to the function: here, one partial derivative per parameter. Pairs of parameters appear in the matrix of second derivatives (the Hessian: each entry differentiates one partial derivative again with respect to another parameter; lesson 7), which is far too large to form for such models.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Jacobians: derivatives of vector-valued functions
question: A linear layer maps 512 inputs to 256 outputs, $z = Wx + b$. What are the shapes of the Jacobian $\partial z/\partial x$ and of the gradient $\partial L/\partial W$ for a scalar loss $L$?
options: Both 512 x 256
Jacobian 256 x 512; dL/dW 256 x 512, the shape of W
Jacobian 256 x 512; dL/dW 512 x 1
Jacobian 512 x 512; dL/dW 256 x 256
explain: The Jacobian has one row per output (256) and one column per input (512), and it equals $W$, which is $256 \times 512$. The gradient of a scalar loss with respect to $W$ has one entry per weight, so it matches $W$'s shape; it is the outer product of the 256-entry $\partial L/\partial z$ with the 512-entry $x$.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files
question: In bash, `echo {1,2}-$((3+4))` prints what?
explain: Brace expansion runs first and makes two words, `1-$((3+4))` and `2-$((3+4))`. Arithmetic expansion then evaluates each to 7.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Searching and transforming text: grep, regex, find, sed and awk
question: In a folder containing `a.txt` and `b.txt`, `find . -name *.txt` fails with an error. Why?
options: find does not accept globs after -name
-name needs the full path rather than a pattern
The shell expands `*.txt` to `a.txt b.txt` before find runs, so find gets an extra argument it cannot parse
find refuses to search the current directory
explain: Expansion happens before the command runs (lesson 3). find receives `-name a.txt b.txt`; -name takes exactly one pattern, so `b.txt` is a stray argument. `find . -name '*.txt'` passes the pattern through for find to match against every file name in the tree.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours
question: With window $c = 2$, how many (center, context) pairs does the 6-word sentence *the cat sat on the mat* produce?
explain: Edge words have fewer neighbours: positions 0 and 5 get 2 context words each, positions 1 and 4 get 3, positions 2 and 3 get 4. That is 2 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 18. The naive 6 x 4 = 24 forgets that the window is cut off at the sentence edges.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
question: A teammate reports that *king - man + woman* returns *king* in your system. What is the best first check?
options: Retrain with a larger dimension
Switch from cosine to Euclidean distance
Whether the nearest-neighbour search excludes the three query words, as the original evaluation did
Increase the number of negative samples
explain: Returning an input word is the expected behaviour when inputs are not excluded: Nissim et al. measured 0.21 accuracy unconstrained vs 0.74 constrained on the same vectors.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Beyond words: autoencoders and the InfoNCE loss
question: A contrastive model is trained with InfoNCE over $N = 256$ candidates per anchor. What is the most mutual information, in nats, that the bound $\log N - L_N$ can certify, however good the encoder?
explain: $L_N \ge 0$, so $\log N - L_N \le \ln 256 = 5.545$ nats (8 bits). 1.386 is $\ln 4$, the limit for 4 candidates; to certify more, use more candidates.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
question: A 13B-parameter FP16 model runs on the same A100 at batch 1. Roughly what is the best-case decode speed?
options: About 78 tokens/s
About 152 tokens/s, the same as 7B
About 24,000 tokens/s
It depends only on the prompt length
explain: Weights are 26 GB; 26 GB / 2.039 TB/s is about 12.8 ms per token, or about 78 tokens/s. Decode time scales with bytes read, so twice the parameters means roughly half the speed.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: When one GPU is not enough: tensor parallelism and the decode floor
question: Which way of using more GPUs lowers the latency of a single decoding request?
options: Tensor parallelism, because each GPU reads only a slice of every layer's weights for the same token
Data parallelism, because there are more copies of the model
Pipeline parallelism, because the layers run on different GPUs
None of them can, since decode is memory-bound
explain: Only tensor parallelism splits the work of one token across GPUs at the same moment, adding their bandwidth together. Data parallelism serves more requests; pipeline parallelism makes one token visit the stages one after another.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat
question: In `addq (%rdi,%rcx,8), %rax`, why is rcx multiplied by 8?
options: Because x86-64 has 8 general-purpose registers
Because the loop is unrolled 8 times
Because memory is read in 8-bit units
Because each long is 8 bytes, so element i starts 8 x i bytes after a
explain: Memory is addressed in bytes, and a long is 8 bytes on x86-64 Linux. a[i] therefore lives at address a + 8 x i. The CPU computes that address as part of the instruction (base rdi plus index rcx times scale 8).

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The OS in charge: system calls and sharing the CPU
question: Why does a system call use a trap instruction instead of letting the program jump directly to the kernel's code for write?
options: Jumps cannot reach addresses that large
Trap instructions are faster than jumps
The trap switches to kernel mode and enters only at handlers the kernel registered, so a program cannot run arbitrary kernel code with full privileges
The C library has no way to call functions
explain: If user code could jump anywhere into the kernel with privileges, it could skip permission checks. The trap table, set up at boot in kernel mode, fixes the only entry points, and the mode switch happens in hardware as part of the trap.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From web crawl to training tokens: the pretraining data pipeline
question: Why did Llama 3 find the document mask mattered more in long-context training than in standard 8K pretraining?
options: A 128K-token sequence packs many unrelated documents, so a plain causal mask lets tokens attend to far more unrelated text
Document masks make attention cost linear in sequence length
Long sequences do not use an end-of-text token
The document mask is needed for the learning rate to anneal
explain: With longer windows a token can see many more tokens from other documents, which can distract or teach false dependencies. The mask keeps each prediction conditioned on its own document only. It changes which keys are visible, not the asymptotic cost.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
question: During RLHF, the mean reward keeps rising while the KL from the SFT model shoots up and samples start repeating odd phrases. Which change most directly addresses this?
options: Raise beta, or stop at an earlier checkpoint
Lower beta so the policy can explore more
Lower the PPO clip range to 0
Remove the value model
explain: Rising reward with exploding KL is the signature of the policy exploiting the reward model. A larger beta makes drift more expensive, and earlier checkpoints have less drift. Lowering beta makes it worse; a clip range of 0 stops learning entirely.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Building the index: tokens, sorting and postings
question: After indexing, which statistic for a term equals the length of its postings list?
options: Its collection frequency
Its document frequency
Its largest term frequency
The number of positions stored for it
explain: One posting per document that contains the term, so the list length is df. Collection frequency counts every occurrence, which is the sum of the tf values stored in those postings.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
question: N = 1,000,000 and a term has df = 1,000 and tf = 3 in a document. What is its weight with raw tf, and with sublinear tf 1 + log10(tf)?
explain: idf = log10(1,000,000 / 1,000) = 3. Raw: 3 x 3 = 9. Sublinear: (1 + log10 3) x 3 = 1.477 x 3 = 4.43. Sublinear scaling halves this weight here because three occurrences count as about 1.5.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages
question: Your build prints "undefined reference to `area'". `main.c` already has `#include "square.h"`, which declares `area`. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add another #include "square.h" to area.c
Pass area.c (or area.o) to the link command
Compile main.c with -O2 so the call is inlined
Add the -E flag so the macro is expanded
explain: This message comes from the linker: main.o refers to the symbol area but no object file or library on the command line defines it. Headers only declare. -O2 (optimization level 2) cannot help: the compiler can only inline a body it can see, and main.c never sees area.c. The fix is to give the linker the definition, for example `gcc main.c area.c -o app`.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Integer types and conversions: where -1 > 0u
question: `unsigned char a = 250, b = 10; int s = a + b;` What is s?
options: Undefined behavior, because the sum overflows unsigned char
explain: Integer promotion converts a and b to int before adding, so the sum is computed as int and 260 fits. It would become 4 only if stored back into an unsigned char (260 modulo 256).

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Files and errors: stdio, return codes and errno
options: It tests errno instead of f: errno may be nonzero even though fopen succeeded
Nothing; errno is 0 whenever fopen succeeds
perror needs errno passed as an argument
fopen never sets errno, so the check never fires
explain: errno is meaningful only after a call reports failure, and a successful call is allowed to change it. Test `if (!f)` and only then use errno (through perror). The library never sets errno back to zero for you.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Rust for C programmers: cargo, let, structs, enums and match
question: `parse_port("80x")` runs `let n: u16 = s.trim().parse()?;` and the parse fails. What happens next?
options: `parse_port` returns `Err(...)` to its caller immediately, and `Ok(n)` is never reached
`n` is set to 0 and the function continues
The program panics with an InvalidDigit message
`?` skips the bad character and parses "80"
explain: `?` on an `Err` returns that error from the enclosing function at once, like `return Err(e)`. The caller decides what to do; in the example it prints the debug form of the error. Panicking is what `unwrap()` would do instead.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Ownership in methods and loops: self, &self, &mut self and for
question: A builder type has `fn finish(self) -> Report`, and you call `let r = builder.finish();`. What can you do with `builder` afterwards?
options: Nothing: it was moved into `finish`, so any later use is E0382
Read its fields, since only its methods are consumed
Call `finish` again, because methods can always be called repeatedly
Use it until the end of the scope, where it is dropped
explain: A `self` receiver takes ownership, exactly like passing the value to a function by value. `builder` is moved-from after the call, and the method decided what happened to its contents (here, turning them into a `Report`).

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Closures and threads: moving ownership to another thread
question: Why is `thread::spawn(|| println!("{v:?}"))` rejected when `v` is a local Vec, while calling the same closure directly in `main` works?
options: Closures cannot capture a Vec
`println!` is not thread safe
Vec cannot be used from more than one thread
The new thread may outlive main's local `v`, and `spawn` requires a `'static` closure, which cannot borrow locals
explain: The closure captures `&v`. Called directly, the borrow ends before `v` is dropped. Passed to `spawn`, the thread could still be running after `v` is gone, so the `'static` bound rejects the borrow with E0373. `move` fixes it by giving the thread its own Vec.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
question: Is $f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ guaranteed to satisfy $f(2\mathbf{x}) = 2f(\mathbf{x})$ for every matrix $A$?
options: Only if A is square
Only if A is a rotation
Yes, for every matrix A
No, only if A has no negative entries
explain: Each output component is $\sum_j A_{ij}(2x_j) = 2\sum_j A_{ij}x_j$. Scaling passes through any matrix. This is half of the definition of linearity; the other half is $f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}) = f(\mathbf{x}) + f(\mathbf{y})$.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Orthogonality, projections and least squares
question: Project $\mathbf{b} = [2, 1]$ onto the line through $\mathbf{a} = [1, 1]$. What is $\mathbf{p}$?
explain: $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = 3$ and $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a} = 2$, so $\mathbf{p} = 1.5[1,1]$. Check: $\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p} = [0.5, -0.5]$, whose dot product with $[1,1]$ is 0. $[3,3]$ forgets to divide by $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}$, which you may skip only when $\mathbf{a}$ has length 1.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
question: In the four-point example, you double every target $y_i$ (so the data look like $y = 4x$). Where does the minimum of the MSE move?
options: It stays at 1.99
It moves to 2.99
It moves to 3.98
It moves to 7.96
explain: $w^* = \sum x_i y_i / \sum x_i^2$. Doubling every $y_i$ doubles the numerator, so $w^* = 119.4 / 30 = 3.98$. The minimum loss quadruples too, since every residual doubles before squaring.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Bias and variance: where the U-shaped test curve comes from
question: In the decomposition, what happens to the noise term $\sigma^2$ when you collect 10 times more training data?
options: It stays the same: it belongs to the data, not the model
It falls by a factor of 10
It falls by a factor of $\sqrt{10}$
It becomes part of the variance
explain: The noise is the irreducible randomness in $y$ given $x$; the true function itself pays it (0.09 here). More data shrinks variance, as degree 9 with 100 points showed, but the noise term is unchanged.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Data pitfalls: leakage, distribution shift and baselines
question: A team predicts hospital readmission. Each patient has several visits, and they split the visits randomly into train and validation. Validation AUC is 0.95; on new patients it is 0.70. What is the most likely cause?
options: Visits from the same patient appear on both sides of the split, so validation rewards recognizing patients
The learning rate was too high
AUC is the wrong metric for readmission
The model is underfitting
explain: This is group leakage: patient-specific details let the model match validation visits to training visits of the same person. Splitting by patient (GroupKFold) would have shown the 0.70 before deployment.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: What hidden units compute: hinges, cuts and new features
question: In the XOR network the output unit is $h_1 - 2h_2$, a purely linear function of the hidden activations. How can it classify XOR, which no linear model can?
options: The hidden layer remaps the inputs into features where a straight line separates the classes; the output unit is linear in those features, not in $x$
The output unit secretly applies a ReLU too
It cannot; it only fits the four points by memorizing them
Because the weights were trained, not chosen by hand
explain: Linear in $h$ does not mean linear in $x$. After ReLU the points sit at (0,0), (1,0) and (2,1) in hidden space, where the line $h_1 - 2h_2 = 0.5$ separates them. The weights here were set by hand, so training is not the reason.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backprop for a mini-batch, in matrix form
question: A layer has $W$ of shape 64 x 784 (course convention, units out by units in), the batch $X$ is 32 x 784 and $dZ$ is 32 x 64. Which expression gives $dW$?
options: `X.T @ dZ`
`dZ @ W`
`dZ.T @ X`
`dZ @ X.T`
explain: $dW$ must be 64 x 784, the shape of $W$. Only `dZ.T @ X`, (64 x 32)(32 x 784), produces that, summing over the 32 examples. `X.T @ dZ` gives 784 x 64, the transposed convention. `dZ @ W` is the gradient for the layer's input $X$, and `dZ @ X.T` does not even have matching inner dimensions.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Training a real network: an MLP on handwritten digits
question: The linear model's training and validation losses both flattened near 0.27 to 0.29 by epoch 10. What would help it most?
options: Adding a hidden layer with a nonlinearity, as the MLP does
Training for 100 more epochs
A larger learning rate
A bigger validation set
explain: Both curves flat and close together means underfitting: the model lacks capacity. A linear model can only draw hyperplanes between classes (lesson 1). The hidden layer adds the bends, which is why the MLP reached 0.063 and 0.100 on the same data.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Beyond physical memory: page faults, swapping and replacement
question: With 100 ns memory and 10 ms disk, what is the average memory access time at a 1% miss rate?
options: About 100 microseconds
About 101 nanoseconds
About 10 milliseconds
About 1 microsecond
explain: AMAT = 100 ns + 0.01 x 10 ms = 0.1 us + 100 us = 100.1 us, a thousand times slower than memory. 101 ns would be the result if the miss cost were 100 ns, not 10 ms.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency bugs: atomicity, ordering and deadlock
question: Two threads use the trylock protocol: lock L1, trylock L2, and on failure unlock L1 and start over. The other thread does the same with L2 first. What new problem can appear?
options: Livelock: both keep backing off and retrying without either making progress
Deadlock, because trylock blocks
Starvation of the scheduler
Mutual exclusion is lost
explain: trylock never blocks, so a thread waiting for the second lock never holds the first one for long and deadlock cannot form. But both threads can repeatedly grab one lock each, fail, release and retry in step: livelock. OSTEP suggests a random delay before retrying.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Crash consistency: fsck and journaling
question: In ordered (metadata) journaling, which writes must be complete before the file system issues the TxE commit block?
options: Only TxB
Only the data block Db
The checkpoint of I[v2] and B[v2]
Db at its final location, plus TxB and the journaled metadata
explain: The commit is the point of no return: after it, recovery will replay the metadata. If Db were not on disk yet, the replayed inode could point to garbage, and if the journaled metadata were incomplete, replay would copy garbage. Checkpointing happens after the commit, not before.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Random variables, expected value and variance
question: A large language model (LLM) evaluation has 200 independent questions and the model answers each correctly with probability 0.7. What are the mean and standard deviation of the number correct?
options: Mean 140, standard deviation 42
Mean 140, standard deviation about 6.5
Mean 0.7, standard deviation 0.21
Mean 140, standard deviation 0.46
explain: Binomial with n = 200, p = 0.7: mean np = 140, variance np(1 - p) = 42, so the standard deviation is the square root, about 6.48. Option A forgets the square root. Runs of the same eval can differ by several questions from noise alone.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Estimating parameters from data: maximum likelihood
question: You compute the variance of 4 validation losses with np.var and compare it to a colleague's number computed with pandas on the same 4 values. Theirs is larger. Why?
options: pandas divides by n - 1 = 3, NumPy by n = 4, so theirs is 4/3 as large
pandas uses the population mean instead of the sample mean
NumPy squares the standard deviation twice
One of you has a bug, since variance is uniquely defined
explain: np.var defaults to ddof=0 (divide by n) and pandas Series.var defaults to ddof=1 (divide by n - 1). With 4 values the ratio is 4/3. Neither uses a population mean; both subtract the sample mean.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Power and sample size: planning an A/B test before running it
question: At the same alpha and power, how many users do you need to detect an effect half as large?
options: Twice as many
About 4 times as many
About 1.4 times as many
The same number, since alpha and power are unchanged
explain: The required n scales with 1 over the effect squared, because the standard error shrinks only as 1 / sqrt(n). Half the effect needs about 4 times the users: 3,839 per arm for 2 points but about 14,750 for 1 point (the variance term also shifts slightly).

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Run your own scaling study: sweep, fit, extrapolate, error bars
question: Why did Hoffmann et al. minimize a Huber loss on log loss rather than plain squared error on the loss itself?
options: The log makes a 1 percent miss count equally at every scale, and Huber keeps a few outlier runs from dominating
Huber loss makes L-BFGS converge in a single step
Squared error cannot be minimized with gradients
Taking logs removes the need to fit the constant E
explain: Losses differ across scales, so log residuals put every run on equal footing. Huber is quadratic within delta and linear beyond it, so one bad run pulls with bounded force; Hoffmann et al. found that important for predicting held-out larger runs. E is still fitted, as one of the three LSE terms.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Inference cost, overtraining and where scaling laws break
question: Exact-match accuracy on a task jumps from near 0% to 60% between two model sizes, while per-token loss falls smoothly. What is the most careful reading?
options: The larger model suddenly acquired a new capability that scaling laws cannot describe
The metric is nonlinear: smooth per-token gains compound into an all-or-nothing score, so the jump may be partly a metric effect
The loss measurement must be wrong
The smaller model was undertrained, which fully explains the jump
explain: Schaeffer et al. show that discontinuous metrics like exact match can turn smooth improvement into apparent jumps, and continuous metrics make the trend smooth again. That is why Llama 3 forecast accuracy through NLL first. It does not prove no real change ever happens, but the jump alone is not evidence of one.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Average precision, MAP and MRR: one number for a whole ranking
question: You evaluate a search box that jumps the user straight to a product page (each query has exactly one correct product). Which metric best matches the user's experience?
options: MRR
Recall@1000
MAP over all relevant products
11-point interpolated precision
explain: With exactly one right answer, what matters is how high it appears, which is what reciprocal rank measures. Recall@1000 ignores position. With a single relevant document AP equals RR anyway, and the recall-level machinery of 11-point precision adds nothing.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow
